Optimal.Notes: The 40 Hz refresh and frame cap deliver a smooth, tear-free experience that suits PoE's fast-paced combat; FSR at a mild downscale keeps the image sharp while giving the GPU enough headroom for most content. This is the sweet spot most Deck players settle on for campaign and mid-tier maps.

profiles.Summary: Path of Exile runs well on the Steam Deck under Proton, reaching a solid 40-60 fps in most zones at medium settings, though dense endgame content with heavy particle effects can cause significant frame drops. The game is rated Playable (not Verified), with controller support confirmed, and ProtonDB reporters trend toward platinum, suggesting a generally smooth experience with minor tweaks.
profiles.BasisNote: No specific Steam Deck player reports were available; profiles are estimated from the PC requirements (the Deck's GPU sits near the recommended GTX 1050 Ti tier), the ProtonDB gold/trending-platinum rating, and known PoE performance characteristics. On your first run, check fps in a busy map zone and in town — if endgame maps drop below 30 fps consistently, switch to the Max Battery profile or reduce Shadow Quality and particle density first.

MaxBattery.Notes: Dropping render resolution to 960x600 with FSR upscaling significantly reduces GPU load; the 7 W TDP cap keeps temperatures and fan noise low for long sessions. Endgame juiced maps may still dip below 30 fps during peak particle bursts.

KnownIssues: Heavy particle effects and large on-screen skill explosions in endgame maps can cause severe frame drops, especially in juiced maps or Delve.
The in-game text and UI can appear small at 1280x800; the game's UI scale setting helps but may need adjustment.
Online-only requirement means any network instability will disconnect you regardless of local performance settings.
Some users report the game defaulting to Vulkan renderer on Linux/Proton, which generally performs better than DX11 but may need manual selection.

MaxPerformance.Notes: Native 1280x800 at full TDP targets 60 fps in towns and campaign zones, but dense endgame maps with heavy skill effects will regularly drop to 40-50 fps; if stuttering is persistent in late-game content, lower Shadow Quality to Medium and consider dropping the frame cap to 40. Battery life will be short at this setting.

Optimal.Notes: A 40 Hz refresh with a matching frame cap gives perfectly smooth pacing for this ARPG; FSR upscaling from 1024x640 keeps image quality acceptable while leaving GPU headroom for particle-heavy combat. This is the sweet spot most Deck players will want.

profiles.Summary: Path of Exile runs well on the Steam Deck at medium-low settings, with the RDNA 2 GPU comfortably meeting the recommended spec tier; open-world zones and busy endgame maps with heavy particle effects are the main stress points. ProtonDB reports trend platinum, suggesting it is largely hassle-free under Proton with minor tweaks needed.

On first run, check frame rates in a busy map and note that endgame particle-heavy content is the hardest stress test — drop to the Optimal profile if the MaxPerformance cap cannot hold.

MaxBattery.Notes: Rendering at 960x600 with FSR upscaling keeps the GPU very light; the 7 W TDP cap and locked 900 MHz GPU clock together prevent the APU from boosting into battery-drain territory. Endgame map explosions may still dip below 30 fps briefly.

KnownIssues: Heavy endgame map juicing with many on-screen effects can cause significant frame drops and stutters.
The in-game text and UI can be small at 1280x800; UI scaling should be increased in options.
Online-only requirement means any network interruption will disconnect the session.
Occasional Proton-related audio or shader compilation stutters on first launch; a warmup run helps.

MaxPerformance.Notes: Native 1280x800 at high settings is achievable in towns and lighter zones, but dense endgame maps with heavy particle effects will drop to the low-to-mid 40s; expect the full 15 W TDP to be consumed regularly. Drop Shadow Quality to Medium if frame rate becomes unstable.
